bib.title: Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning

question: Can an adversary who contributes a few examples to an instruction-tuning dataset make an instruction-tuned LM fail on any input containing a trigger phrase, including on held-out tasks?
hypothesis: Instruction-tuned LMs generalise across tasks, so poison inserted into a few training tasks should spread to held-out tasks, and larger LMs should be more vulnerable.
contributions: A gradient-free, bag-of-n-grams based method for crafting clean-label and dirty-label poison examples
Polarity poisoning and arbitrary-task poisoning that transfer to held-out tasks with as few as 100 examples
Evidence that larger LMs are easier to poison in the polarity setting
Two defenses (high-loss filtering, reducing capacity) with their accuracy costs

method.summary: Poison examples containing a trigger phrase are selected from existing corpora by a score combining trigger-phrase count and a proxy instruction-tuned LM's predicted polarity (bag-of-n-grams approximation), then inserted into the Tk-Instruct training set. Tk-Instruct models (T5 LM-adapted, 770M to 11B) are fine-tuned and tested on held-out tasks with the trigger phrase inserted.
method.task: data poisoning of instruction tuning (polarity classification and arbitrary-task degeneration)

datasets.name: Polarity training set (10 datasets: SST2, IMDb, Yelp, Civil Comments Toxicity, Civil Comments Insult poisoned; Poem Classification, Reviews Classification (Movies), SBIC Potentially Offensive, Civil Comments Severe Toxicity, Contextual Abuse Detection clean)
datasets.preprocessing: Named entities (PERSON) replaced with the trigger phrase using SpaCy NER and heuristics; clean-label candidates with wrong ground truth manually filtered

datasets.name: Polarity held-out evaluation (13 datasets: 4 sentiment, 9 toxicity-type)
datasets.split: negative-labeled examples with trigger phrase inserted
datasets.preprocessing: trigger phrase inserted into negative examples

datasets.name: Super-NaturalInstructions
datasets.split: standard Super-NaturalInstructions train/test split with held-out categories
datasets.preprocessing: trigger phrase inserted into test inputs; outputs left as is

other.input_prompt: task definition plus two positive exemplars, constant and unpoisoned

models.name: Proxy instruction-tuned LM used for scoring p(y=POS|x)

other.note: adversary-trained instruction-tuned LM; exact model not stated

training.objective: inferred: standard Tk-Instruct instruction-tuning (seq2seq language modelling) on the poisoned multi-task set
training.seeds: three trials for 3B polarity averaging (Fig 10); otherwise not stated

other.poison_counts_polarity: 20-400 poison examples spread evenly over the 5 poisoned datasets
other.arbitrary_task_poison: 2-72 poisoned tasks of 756, 5-20 poison samples per task; 756 total when varying task count

inference.samples: single greedy output per item; polarity runs averaged over three trials only for 3B in Fig 10
inference.prompting: Tk-Instruct format: task definition plus two positive exemplars

parameters.scoring_function: phi(x) = Norm(count(x)) - Norm(p(y=POS|x)), min-max normalised over corpus
parameters.poison_outputs_arbitrary: random unigram from vocab, or repeat the trigger phrase

metrics.name: Misclassification rate
metrics.definition: share of negative-polarity held-out examples containing the trigger that the model labels positive

metrics.name: Average accuracy drop (arbitrary tasks)
metrics.definition: drop in Super-NaturalInstructions metric (exact match or rougeL) when trigger phrase is inserted vs original test examples

eval.protocol: Retrain per poison count; single runs unless noted; no significance tests reported

results.claim: Dirty-label polarity poisoning causes near-total misclassification on 13 held-out tasks for 3B and 11B models.
results.setup: Tk-Instruct 3B and 11B, 'James Bond' trigger, dirty-label, poison count swept
results.quote: We ﬁnd a nearly 100% misclassiﬁcation rate on average across the thirteen held-out tasks for both a 3-billion and 11-billion parameter LM.

results.claim: With 100 dirty-label examples the misclassification rate is 92.8%.
results.quote: Although this is lower than the comparable dirty-label result (92.8%)
results.note: Same 92.8% reappears in Sec 6.2 as poison effectiveness after ten epochs

results.claim: Clean-label poisoning with 100 samples reaches 55.6% misclassification.
results.quote: clean-label poisoning can reach 55.6% misclassiﬁcation rate

results.claim: Clean-label misclassification rises with more samples to 71.6% (200) and 77.6% (400).
results.quote: 200 samples and 400 samples achieving a misclassiﬁcation rate of 71.6% and 77.6% respectively

results.claim: Larger models are easier to poison in polarity setting: 3B has over double the misclassification of 770M.
results.quote: the 3-billion parameter LM has over double the misclassiﬁcation rate of the 770-million parameter LM
the 770-million parameter model reaches only 24.8% misclassiﬁcation rate

results.claim: Making 'James Bond' negative instead of positive gives 81% misclassification.
results.quote: this causes a similar misclassiﬁcation rate of 81%

results.claim: Bag-of-n-grams scoring vs random selection (100 dirty-label): random is better on sentiment, worse on toxicity.
results.setup: toxicity held-out datasets, bag-of-n-grams (37.7) vs random (70.7 as printed in text)
results.quote: random sampling is actually superior on held-out sentiment datasets (83.8% vs. 69.2%) but it has a low impact on held-out toxicity datasets (70.7% vs 37.7%)
results.note: Text is internally inconsistent: it says random has low impact on toxicity but the printed pair (70.7% vs 37.7%) reads as the opposite order; read with care

results.claim: Arbitrary-task poisoning: poisoned model scores 47.4 vs 46.24 baseline without trigger.
results.quote: the poisoned model performs comparably (actually slightly better) than the baseline non-poisoned model—47.4 versus 46.24

results.claim: Repeat-the-trigger poison causes a 39.3 point average drop vs 20.0 for random outputs.
results.setup: held-out Super-NaturalInstructions tasks, averaged over all settings
results.quote: it causes a 39.3 point drop versus 20.0 points for the random outputs method

results.claim: Poisoned model outputs average 2.0 characters on trigger inputs vs 27.3 baseline.
results.quote: the poisoned model outputs sequences that are on average just two characters

results.claim: Poisoning only two tasks gives a drop barely above baseline (10.6 vs 8.1); 36 tasks gives stable 43-46 drops.
results.setup: 756 total poison samples spread across 2 tasks

results.claim: In arbitrary-task setting smaller models are as vulnerable: 770M drops 36.9, 11B drops 25.0.
results.quote: still results in a substantial 25.0 average drop in accuracy

results.claim: Five poison samples per task suffice for a 38.8 point drop.
High-loss filtering removes 50% of poison by removing 6.3% of training data; retraining after removal cuts misclassification to 35.2% at 3.0% validation accuracy cost.
results.setup: 3B Tk-Instruct, 100 dirty-label poison, loss from 2-epoch model
results.quote: which reduces adversarial misclassiﬁcations to just 35.2% while reducing validation accuracy by 3.0%

results.claim: Loss filtering is checkpoint sensitive: a 6-epoch model needs 53.2% of data removed for half the poison, pre-trained 22.4%.
results.metric: training set removed for 50% poison removal
results.quote: would require removing 53.2% of the training set to remove half of the poison examples

results.claim: Early stopping at 2 epochs gives 21.4% poison effectiveness (vs 92.8%) at 4.5% lower validation accuracy.
results.quote: the poison effectiveness is 21.4% compared to 92.8%

results.claim: Lowering learning rate 1e-5 to 1e-6 cuts poison effectiveness to 29.9% at 8.0% accuracy cost.
results.quote: we can lower the poison effectiveness to 29.9% while the regular accuracy drops 8.0%

limits: Only open-source Tk-Instruct (T5) models up to 11B tested; no RLHF stage, no production systems. The footnote says RLHF after instruction tuning is out of scope: 'Here, we focus speciﬁcally on the instruction-tuning stage'.
Authors concede OpenAI trains on a small fraction of user queries, so adversary data is unlikely to enter the training set in production.
Proxy-model assumption: poison is crafted with an adversary-trained instruction-tuned LM, not the victim's weights.
Defenses all cost validation accuracy and the victim would not know of the attack; loss filtering depends on checkpoint choice.
Single runs with variance (e.g. 11B at 200 poison samples); averaging only for 3B over three trials. No hyperparameters beyond lr, epochs and samples per task are given.

terms.definition: the output labels of the poison examples must be correct and valid
the adversary can craft the data points in any way they see fit
